sources.title: Official biography: birth, education, diplomatic, parliamentary and presidential chronology
sources.findings: Read selected official biographical paragraphs on birth, education, diplomatic appointments, Senate service and presidential chronology. They give Almaty, 17 May 1953; MGIMO graduation 1975; Beijing language training 1983–1984; Russian Diplomatic Academy graduation 1992. Language training is not an additional degree. Career dates include deputy foreign minister 1992, first deputy 1993, foreign minister 1994, deputy prime minister March 1999, prime minister October 1999, state secretary/foreign minister January 2002, Senate 2007–2011 and again from October 2013 to 2019. The English biography incorrectly calls the UN rank Deputy Secretary-General; the UN’s own record establishes Under-Secretary-General instead. Presidential succession, June election and oath, and November 2022 vote share are kept separate. No present party leadership inferred from historical posts.

sources.title: Former Directors-General: Tokayev 2011–2013 and Under-Secretary-General rank
sources.findings: Read Tokayev’s own section of the UN Geneva former-directors list, not adjacent biographies. It records 2011–2013 service, a March 2011 appointment announcement, Under-Secretary-General rank and personal representation of the secretary-general at the Conference on Disarmament. He was not the UN Deputy Secretary-General. The account also confirms October 1999 prime-ministerial appointment with parliamentary consent and January 2002 resignation. Do not assign another director’s birthplace or dates to him; no exact arrival day established from this section.

sources.title: 20 March 2019 succession following Nazarbayev’s resignation
sources.findings: Read Reuters’ short 20 March 2019 succession account on Euronews and its dated oath caption. Nazarbayev resigned the previous day and Tokayev actually assumed the presidency on 20 March. The contemporary prediction of serving until April 2020 is not copied as subsequent history: an early election occurred in June 2019. Senate chairmanship and June election/oath dates are supported by the official biography, not falsely attributed to this short article, which does not mention the Senate in its body.

sources.title: 7 January 2022 statement announcing shoot-to-kill orders without warning
sources.findings: Read the relevant 7 January 2022 Reuters article syndicated by MarketScreener. Tokayev announced lethal-force orders without warning, rejected talks with people he called terrorists, and said requested CSTO troops were temporarily present. His terrorism and bandit descriptions are attributed accusations, not independently established descriptions of all protesters. The claimed 20,000 attackers and uncertain death totals are not adopted. No independent operational order text or complete casualty investigation was reviewed.

sources.title: World Report 2026, events of 2025: accountability for January 2022 abuses
sources.findings: Read the selected accountability sections of Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026, explicitly covering events of 2025. It records six police officers convicted of torture on 17 January, sentences upheld in June, and broader investigation shortcomings despite multiple convictions. This avoids claiming that nobody was punished. ODIHR trial-monitoring and UN Human Rights Committee concerns are reported through HRW; underlying full judgments and committee records were not independently read. No personal criminal conviction of Tokayev or exact current death/prisoner tally is asserted.

sources.title: 2022 result determination, registration and oath scheduled for 26 November
sources.findings: Read the electoral commission decision determining the November 2022 election outcome, registering the president-elect and setting the oath for 26 November. The vote itself was 20 November. The 81.31% figure is supported by the official biography and additionally read Kazinform inauguration account; the displayed commission decision was not misdescribed as showing that percentage. A planned oath date alone is not evidence of actual attendance; the speech and dated report establish the ceremony occurred.

sources.title: 2022 inauguration speech: single seven-year term and stated reform programme
sources.findings: Read selected opening and term-limit passages of the presidential inauguration speech. It states a single seven-year presidential term following that year’s amendments. Claims of comprehensive renewal and public support are the president’s political evaluation, not independently audited democratic outcomes. The dated 26 November Kazinform ceremony report separately confirms the actual event. No personal guarantee of a future departure date or interpretation of every later transitional clause is made.

sources.publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
sources.title: 21 November 2022 observation statement: efficient preparation but lack of competition
sources.findings: Read the OSCE/ODIHR 21 November 2022 preliminary election-observation statement’s relevant assessment. Preparation was efficient, but the political environment lacked meaningful competition, fundamental freedoms and eligibility rules remained restrictive, and the incumbent faced no meaningful challenge. This is an observer assessment, not an endorsement of fairness or a criminal ruling. The complete final-report PDF was not reviewed; high official vote share does not resolve the competition concerns.

sources.title: 2026 constitutional text: presidential term, vice-president, Kurultai and transitional provisions
sources.findings: Read selected provisions of the 2026 constitution on the government English-language page: Article 43 seven-year presidential term; Article 49 presidential appointment of a vice-president with Kurultai majority consent; Articles 52–53 legislative authority and 145-member chamber; Articles 94–95 commencement on 1 July and transition from the old parliament. A single chamber and vice-presidency are institutional changes, not proof of democratization. Commencement is distinct from later elections and appointments. No certified translation comparison, complete constitutional adjudication or claim about a future term reset is made.

sources.title: Official results of 15 March 2026 constitutional referendum
sources.findings: Read the commission’s official 15 March 2026 referendum result. It reports 73.12% turnout and 87.15% approval among participants; approval is not the percentage of all eligible voters. The public profile uses the referendum date without importing unsupported unanimity claims. Adoption, promulgation and legal commencement are separate events; no unverified signature date is supplied.

sources.title: 1 July 2026 notice confirming entry into force of the new constitution
sources.findings: Read the Constitutional Court’s 1 July 2026 notice confirming that the new constitution entered into force and replaced the 1995 constitution that day. This is actual commencement evidence, not merely a future announcement. Institutional claims about stronger rights and accountability are not independent evidence that those outcomes have already been achieved.

sources.title: 2026 Kurultai election factsheet: 23 August vote and transition to a single chamber
sources.findings: Read the diplomatic mission’s factsheet, including the opening that explicitly records the first unicameral Kurultai election on 23 August 2026, 145 seats, and replacement of the Senate/Mazhilis structure. It is a government account; its summaries of observer opinions are not independent reading of those reports. The page published 31 August retains prospective wording about a first session scheduled for 28 August, so that wording is not used to prove actual first-session attendance. No public party seat totals, current party leadership or completed vice-presidential appointment is inferred.

sources.title: 30 June 2026 account of constitutional transition and succession debate
sources.findings: Read selected Reuters paragraphs dated 30 June 2026 on the new constitution taking effect the following day and the political-transition debate. Analytical speculation about succession is not a confirmed plan. The subsequent Constitutional Court notice verifies actual commencement, and the later official factsheet confirms the August election; future-tense expectations in the June account are not treated as those later events having happened already.

sources.title: 16 November 2026 completed meeting with energy minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov
sources.findings: Read the presidential account of the completed 16 November 2026 meeting with energy minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, including the heating season, energy production and investment projects. This establishes recent actual activity. Reported production growth is a ministerial/government account, not an independently audited economic outcome; plans for refinery projects are not completed construction. Public text avoids unverified production totals.

sources.title: 16 November 2026 introduction of new KNB chairman Marat Irmenov
sources.findings: Read the 16 November 2026 presidential account of the completed meeting with National Security Committee leadership and presentation of new chairman Marat Irmenov. This committee is distinct from the Security Council chaired by the president. Earlier meetings with the former security chief do not establish that he still held office on the cutoff date. Reform and anticorruption demands are directions, not proof that reforms have succeeded.

sources.title: 16 November 2026 security-chief replacement and attributed corruption-investigation context
sources.findings: Read selected accessible Reuters paragraphs dated 16 November 2026 on the security-chief replacement and a spokesperson’s attributed explanation involving the arrest of sovereign-wealth-fund head Nurlan Zhakupov. Suspicion or arrest is not conviction, and these allegations are not added to the public profile. A later reopen returned an access error; only the previously accessible selected passages are claimed as read. The official presidential meeting record directly supports the public personnel-change statement.
